Flash of Green

Green Bee-eater · Wilpattu National Park, Sri Lanka

In the wild forests of Wilpattu National Park, there is a little bird that shines like a jewel: the green bee-eater.

He is small, no longer than a pencil, but impossible to miss. His feathers are a bright, glowing green, with a dark stripe across his eyes like a little mask. And from the middle of his tail grow two long, thin feathers that trail behind him like streamers.

The green bee-eater can be found across much of Asia, but the ones in Sri Lanka are special. They belong to their very own Sri Lankan variety, found nowhere else. Of all the bee-eaters on the island, he is the most common, and the one you are most likely to meet.

His name tells you what he loves to eat. Bee-eaters hunt bees, wasps and other flying insects, and they catch nearly all of them in the air. He waits on a branch, watching. When an insect flies past, he darts out, snatches it mid-flight, and swoops back to his perch.

But a bee can sting, and the bee-eater knows it. So before he eats, he does something clever. He holds the insect in his beak and beats it against the branch, again and again, until the sting is gone. Only then does he enjoy his meal.

When it is time to raise a family, bee-eaters don't build a nest in a tree. Instead, they dig a long tunnel into a sandy bank, and lay their eggs safely at the very end of it.

So the next time you see a flash of green zip through the air, look closely. It might just be a bee-eater, catching his lunch.
